newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt, Amoco talk pipelines, prices for Turkey gas.
newsitem.headline: Egypt, Amoco talk pipelines, prices for Turkey gas.

text.p: Egypt and the U.S. company Amoco Corp are working on terms of a deal to supply natural gas to Turkey, and one option is to build a pipeline to catch a larger share of the European market, officials said on Wednesday.

"We've been diligently examining that potential business opportunity with the Turkish," said Robert Sheppard, President and General Manager of Amoco Egypt. "It is still progressing as one of the options for exporting Egyptian gas into near region markets," he told reporters at an economic conference.

He was referring to a memorandum of understanding signed in November by Egypt, Amoco and the Turkish company Botas which sees Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation (EGPC) supplying about 10 billion cubic metres of liquefied natural gas (LNG) to Turkey a year.
Amoco, which said it expected to start deliveries in 2001, is the largest foreign investor in Egypt with more than $7.5 billion in Egypt's energy sector, Sheppard said.
He said in a speech that the company continued to invest more than $175 million a year and had "plans for staying in the business of producing oil in Egypt for a long time".
Amoco Egypt and EGPC this week named Citibank as financial adviser to the $1.2 billion Turkish LNG project. Sheppard said the move meant that they were closer to deciding on terms.
"It made sense to bring them in pretty early. A lot of the issues you're going to grapple with to see if this project is real are going to be how can you finance it," he said.
Egyptian Oil Minister Hamdi el-Banbi said in April a new liquefaction plant, for which a site was chosen west of Port Said, would handle four billion cubic metres of gas a year.
Sheppard said that substantial investments would not be made until there was a buyer and that there were still costs and volumes to work out with the Turkish side.
"It has cost implications...those are some of the things we are focusing on," he said.

"I think that their strategy is wanting to diversify their sources, and also the delivery systems. Pipeline is one element but LNG is another. They've indicated to us that they want about 30 percent of their total energy requirements via LNG."
He said they were starting talks on gas pricing. "That can be very protracted...I think we'll know within the next six months whether this is a deal or not."
EGPC Chairman Abdel Khalek Ayad told the conference that a pipeline to take natural gas from Egypt to Turkey remained under discussion, alongside plans to export LNG by tanker.
"We are studying seriously a pipeline to stretch up to Turkey or to any place in Europe. This study is undergoing so we are trying to capture the expanding gas market in Europe."
